title: Halloween, farm style.
summary: Skeleton glasses, corn sifting, a farm ride and memories of Connor’s Halloween Party at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island.
search: The journal Warren, Rhode Island A Halloween family field note Skeleton glasses. Cookie in hand. Not a bad way to start a Halloween story. A family afternoon at Frerichs Farm Halloween, farm style. A cookie, some spectacular skeleton glasses, corn to sift—and a farm that made a special Halloween invitation to autistic families. An AUsome Life · Published October 7, 2026 From an earlier family visit Some photographs bring back a whole afternoon. These are the ones with a yellow Black Panther shirt, a bit of Halloween mischief, and the three of us sitting close together in the October sunshine. They were taken at Frerichs Farm in Warren, Rhode Island. They still make me smile. Our afternoon Connor’s Halloween Party The farm ride More photographs Map & visit details Access & sensory notes Opened from the family album A little skeleton and a lot of personality. The Halloween glasses deserve their own place in the album. White plastic bones frame a tiny skull, held up in front of one eye. A cookie is being kept very firmly in the other hand. The shirt is bright yellow, and absolutely none of the photograph looks like it needed organizing by an adult. Behind him, people are sitting under a big tent. The grass is green, the light is lovely, and it is the kind of unplanned photograph that ends up meaning more than the ones we spend ten minutes trying to pose. For us, these little moments are the story. Not how many attractions we did, or how much we fitted into an afternoon. Just the part we actually enjoyed. Pour, sift, watch, repeat. A good activity does not have to hurry. All three of us together in the autumn sun. A small activity, a real memory There was a table full of sand and corn. The sifting station was a wonderfully simple thing: a shallow tabletop, scattered corn kernels, a wooden screen, and a paper cup for pouring. It offered something to do with your hands and something interesting to watch happen. I love that we kept a picture of it. Sometimes the most absorbing stop of the day is not the grand attraction. It is an ordinary little activity that makes sense immediately, with no instructions required. A small study in autumn. Original editorial illustration. The invitation that mattered Connor’s Halloween Party. Frerichs Farm has hosted a special gathering called Connor’s Halloween Party , created for people on the autism spectrum and their families. It has been offered free of charge, with an RSVP, as a chance for families to enjoy some autumn fun together. That intention is part of why I wanted this farm in our family journal. A place can have pumpkins, wagons, treats and games, but there is something extra meaningful about an event that deliberately says to families like ours: this day is for you, too. Previous descriptions of the party mention activities such as the Western Town, pirate ship, bubbles, a scavenger hunt, a bouncy house and food. Activities can change by year, and a designated autism event is not a guarantee that every sound, surface or crowd will suit every person. Still, the invitation itself matters. A note on dates: Despite being a memory from an earlier visit, this is not necessarily a discontinued event. Frerichs Farm listed Connor’s Halloween for October 3, 2026 (rain date October 4). That date has passed; check the farm’s official party page and calendar for any future celebration and RSVP details. In the middle of it all Three of us, a patch of sun. We took several family selfies, and not one needed to be perfect. In one, our son looks away from the camera. In another, he turns toward us. The sun makes its own plans. We were there together. That is the picture I wanted to keep. The bright orange railings behind us, the blue jackets, the rows of white tents in the distance—those details make this feel like a specific day, not just a generic autumn outing. A second photograph from the same few sunny minutes. Little pieces of the day The camera kept rolling. There are a few short videos from the farm ride, too: a look at the tractor, an orange railing against the sky, and the happy disorder of everybody trying to get a view. Check which activities are included in general admission and which require a separate fee or registration. Farm calendar ↗ The useful details A little planning makes room for the good part. Ask about the ground underfoot. Our photos show outdoor grass and a sandy play station. Ask about the route from parking to activities, wet-weather surfaces and any firm or step-free alternatives for strollers, wheelchairs and visitors who prefer steadier footing. Ask what the ride actually involves. If the tractor or pumpkin ride is operating, ask about loading, how long it lasts, how loud it may be, seating and whether someone can choose to watch instead. Previewing a short video can help make the sequence more predictable. Find the quiet route out. Outdoor events can still have crowds, music and unexpected noises. Ask whether there is a less busy arrival time, room to step away, and a straightforward route back to the car if a break is needed. Plan communication and care needs. Keep familiar communication supports close, with a simple way to say “more,” “break” or “finished.” Ask about restrooms, accessible facilities, food options, supervision requirements and any other practical support your family needs. These are planning questions, not verified statements about current accessibility accommodations or sensory provisions. Please check directly with Frerichs Farm before visiting. Before you go The small, sensible list. Confirm the event, RSVP, weather plan, tickets and activity availability. Check parking, paths, restroom access and stroller or mobility needs. Preview any ride, costume or activity that might be unfamiliar. Pack layers, familiar snacks or required food, and communication and calming supports. Give yourselves permission to enjoy one thing really well and call it a lovely day. The photograph I come back to is still the one with the cookie and the skull glasses. There is no grand lesson in it. Just a child having an October afternoon his own way, and a place that thought about welcoming families who are not always included in the usual invitations. I'm glad we went. And I'm very glad we kept the photographs. Family photographs and three short home videos from an earlier visit; exact visit date not supplied. title: A scoop, a phone, and a choice.
summary: How we used photographs and AI to make a visual ice cream flavor choice board at Rancatore's in Lexington, Massachusetts.
search: The journal / Lexington, Massachusetts / Accessible outings A family field note · Rancatore’s ice cream A scoop, a phone, and a choice. How a few photographs at Ranc’s became an on-the-spot visual choice board for James. By An AUsome Life October 7, 2026 Lexington, MA Our real photograph An ice cream cone, a brick-lined passage, and a photograph from our Lexington outing. The little story Photo → choice board The cone question Try it yourself Our photos An ordinary afternoon, with a new idea Some families make visual supports at their kitchen table. On this afternoon, I wondered if I could make one at the ice cream counter. We were heading to Rancatore’s in downtown Lexington—Ranc’s, as we call it—and I had my phone with me. James, my 14-year-old son, is autistic and non-speaking. He communicates in ways that include pointing and using his iPad, so clear pictures are part of our everyday life. We had already made a little visual board to choose where to go. Ranc’s, Cookie Monstah, and Wilson Farm each had their own picture. Once we reached the ice cream shop, there was another decision waiting for us: the flavors. Rather than try to recite the entire case out loud, I took photographs of the actual displays and shared them with AI. Could it turn what was in front of us into pictures James could consider on the spot? We ended up with a photo just outside, an ice cream cone in hand. It is a reminder of what the exercise was for: not a perfect piece of design, but an ordinary afternoon with room for James’s choices. From the family notebook The simple idea. No elaborate equipment. No printer in the car. Just the phone already in my hand and a tool that could help organize the options. 01 Photograph the real options. 02 Create a picture-based board. 03 Check it, simplify it, and offer the choice. The support is new. James’s own communication methods are not. A small experiment, right at the counter From the flavor case to the flavor board. These are the real photographs and the original combined choice board we made during our outing. 01 / The source photograph Real We started with what was physically in the shop, not a generic ice cream menu. 02 / The visual choice board AI The complete combined cone-and-flavor choice board from our outing, in its original arrangement. The AI-illustrated flavors still need checking against the actual case. A helpful distinction: the photographs document what we saw. The AI illustrations translate those choices into a visual format. They are not a verified menu. A cup or a cone. Original editorial illustration. Before the ice cream counter First we chose where to go. We started with a visual destination board: Cookie Monstah in Burlington, Ranc’s in Lexington and Wilson Farm in Lexington. Each place had a familiar storefront picture rather than a generic picture of a cookie or an ice cream. Then, at Ranc’s, we made the combined cone-and-flavor board shown above. Its original layout keeps three cone choices at the top and the labeled flavors below, so we can ask one clear question at a time. The technology wasn’t making the choice for James. It was helping us show him the choices. Our original three-place destination storyboard, without redesigning it. A few things I learned Fast doesn’t mean finished. The AI was quick, but it wasn't automatically right. It can invent a flavor, misread a handwritten label, or make a beautifully crowded page. Our large flavor board was a useful first pass, but for actual use, a shorter selection might be far easier to navigate. The real photos were important because they gave us something concrete to check. And while the board was new, it was never meant to replace James’s established AAC supports or his ability to say no, ask for something different, or take a break. Sometimes the best visual is simply the photograph you already took. Save this idea for your next outing A prompt to try. “Use these photos to create a simple visual choice board. Show only the options that are actually available. Use large, recognizable pictures, clear labels, and separate the flavor choice from the cone choice. Do not invent items.” Before using it, check the names and pictures, remove anything unavailable, and make sure the layout suits the person who will use it. Good for: ice cream shops, bakeries, cafés, farm stands, playgrounds—anywhere the options change from day to day. From our camera roll The photographs behind the board. Unaltered-in-content photos from our visit, not stock images or AI depictions of the shop. The shop counter and the illuminated case. More of the case, from a second angle. A look toward the windows at the end of the counter. The part worth remembering A scoop of ice cream is an ordinary pleasure. A chance to choose it for yourself should be ordinary, too.
